Modern.tagline: Marseille soap. 72% olive oil. Nothing else.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Seventy-Two is the documented minimum olive-oil percentage required for authentic Marseille soap by the 1688 Edict of Colbert. Spelled out, the number reads as a brand mark — distinctive, ownable, and rooted in a verifiable specification.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern bar soap has split into the design-DTC cohort (Public Goods, Beekman 1802) and the heritage cohort (Marius Fabre, Compagnie de Provence). The opening is for a modern brand that anchors to a single specification — the 72% olive-oil minimum — and runs the catalog from there.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Marius Fabre (marius-fabre.com) holds the heritage Marseille peer slot. Compagnie de Provence (compagniedeprovence.com) plays the modern Marseille middle. Savon Stories (savonstories.com) sits in the considered modern peer position. We sit alongside Compagnie de Provence with sharper single-spec anchoring.
Modern.positioningStatement: A modern Marseille-format soap brand built around the 72% olive-oil minimum.

targetAudience.primary: 28 to 50. Buys for the household. Reads ingredient lists. Replaces shower gels with bar soap.

dos: Print the spec on the front of the bar
Name the cauldron and the saponifier

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark — Seventy-Two set in a precise modern grotesque, with '72' as a tonal mark used alone on the bar.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Jean-Baptiste Colbert was the 17th-century French finance minister whose 1688 Edict mandated the 72% olive-oil Marseille soap standard. Olive is the foundational ingredient. The pair reads as a heritage savonnerie with an aristocratic founding-document anchor — without using the trademarked 'Marseille' name as the lead.
Luxury.story: Colbert & Olive is a small French savonnerie founded in 1894 in Salon-de-Provence, run by the founder's great-grandchildren. The catalog runs to eleven bars, each saponified in the original copper cauldrons of the maison.
Luxury.industrySummary: Heritage savonnerie brands are rare and remain among the most premium bar-soap presentations available. There is space for a small French maison operating in the original 1688-spec tradition.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Marius Fabre (marius-fabre.com) is the institutional Marseille peer. Le Sérail (le-serail.com) holds the heritage Marseille slot. Savon de Marseille — Fer à Cheval (savon-de-marseille.com) plays in the heritage middle. We belong with Le Sérail in the small heritage savonnerie category.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A French heritage savonnerie with eleven bars saponified in the original copper cauldrons since 1894.

targetAudience.primary: 40 to 70. Buys for the household across years. Travels to Provence. Re-orders by mail.

dos: Address customers in formal French and English
Reference the 1688 Edict and the founding year
donts: Maintain a social-media presence beyond a quiet archive

Luxury.logoDirection: A serif wordmark — Colbert & Olive in a classical book serif with a small embossed olive-branch mark.

typography.primary: A traditional book serif for the wordmark and printed catalogue
typography.secondary: An engraver's italic for the founding year

Minimal.brandNameRationale: 72/28 is the documented Marseille saponification ratio: 72% olive oil, 28% water-and-lye system. The slash makes it read as a working specification mark, like a parts code. The brand is the ratio.
Minimal.industrySummary: Bar soap has accumulated scent libraries, gift bundles, exfoliant variants, and seasonal collections. There's an opening for a brand that ships one bar at one ratio.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most bar-soap brands fail this purity test. The closest peers in spirit are some single-bar Japanese bath brands and certain pharmacy-counter Marseille bricks.
Minimal.positioningStatement: One bar. One ratio. One price.

targetAudience.primary: Adults who use bar soap daily and want one good unscented bar.
behaviors: Re-buys the same bar for years

dos: Show the bar, the ratio, the price

Minimal.logoDirection: 72/28 set in a single-weight grotesque, tracked tight, used at small scale on the bar itself.

typography.rationale: One face. The wrapper, the spec card, and the receipt share the same mark.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Marseille names the documented French saponification tradition (1688 Edict) without claiming the protected appellation alone. Soap Works follows the heritage industrial naming convention (Sheffield Cutlery Works, Solingen Blade Works). The pair reads as a serious manufacturing operator already on the procurement panel at major retailers.
Corporate.industrySummary: Bar soap manufacturing for hotel groups, hospitality chains, retail private-label, and brand licensees is a B2B category dominated by a handful of large saponifiers (Compagnie de Provence operations, Savon de Marseille industrial cohort). The opening is a mid-tier operator with Marseille-spec discipline and retail-grade reliability.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Compagnie de Provence (compagniedeprovence.com) is the institutional peer at scale. Fer à Cheval (savon-de-marseille.com) holds the heritage Marseille industrial slot. Le Sérail (le-serail.com) plays in the smaller heritage middle. Marius Fabre (marius-fabre.com) sits in the family-operator peer position. We sit closer to Fer à Cheval with a broader hospitality and private-label offering.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Marseille-spec bar soap manufacturing for hospitality, retail private-label, and brand licensees.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Laurel oil is the defining ingredient of Aleppo soap — the 8th-century olive-and-laurel formula widely cited as the world's oldest continuously made soap. Bath House frames the brand as a place, not just a product. The pair reads as a warm, character-driven house with a documented ancient anchor.
Creative.manifesto: Most soap brands whisper. Beige labels. Calm voices. We made Laurel Bath House because the actual experience of a long bath at the end of a long week is loud, warm, and very specific. The brand is the bath. Bring a book.
Creative.industrySummary: Bar-soap branding has been quiet, ethereal, beige, and slightly precious. There's room for one that's loud, warm, character-driven, and serious about the bath itself.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Dr. Squatch (drsquatch.com) does the loud-DTC middle. Beekman 1802 (beekman1802.com) holds the narrative-heritage peer slot. Outlaw Soaps (outlawsoaps.com) sits in the character-driven peer position. We sit warmer and more bath-room than any of them.
Creative.positioningStatement: A bar-soap brand for the long Friday-night bath.
